deep.reconstruction:
§57 of Ramanujan's unpublished continuation of 'Highly composite numbers'. Here he generalises the divisor function to a real exponent and sets up the maximal-order problem.

(1) Definition. For real r, define d_r(N) by ζ(s)^{1+r} = Σ_{N≥1} d_r(N) N^{-s}. With this convention d_1 = d, the usual divisor function. In modern notation d_r = d_{1+r}, the generalised divisor function d_z with z = 1+r.

(2) Formula (295). [My filled step:] From the Euler product ζ(s)^{1+r} = ∏_p (1-p^{-s})^{-(1+r)}, the binomial series gives the coefficient of p^{-as} as
binom(a+r, a) = (1+r)(2+r)···(a+r)/a! = ∏_{λ=1}^{a} (1 + r/λ).
By multiplicativity, for N = ∏_ν p_ν^{a_ν}:
d_r(N) = ∏_ν ∏_{λ=1}^{a_ν} (1 + r/λ).

(3) Special values.
- d_{-1}(N) = 0 (since ζ^0 = 1).
- d_0(N) = 1 (since ζ^1 has all coefficients 1).
- d_1(N) = d(N).

(4) Bound (296). For -1 ≤ r ≤ 0 every factor lies in [0,1]. The λ=1 factor of each prime is 1+r. Hence d_r(N) ≤ (1+r)^{ω(N)} ≤ 1+r.

(5) Primes and unboundedness. For a prime p, d_r(p) = 1+r for every r. For r > 0, d_r(p_1···p_k) = (1+r)^k → ∞, so d_r(N) is unbounded.

(6) Shape of the maximisers (r > 0). Because the factors 1+r/λ decrease in λ, a number maximising d_r should have exponents that do not increase with the prime. So N = ∏ p^{a_p}, with a_p ≥ λ exactly when p ≤ x_λ. Then:
- N = exp(ϑ(x_1) + ϑ(x_2) + ···);
- d_r(N) = ∏_λ (1 + r/λ)^{π(x_λ)}.

(7) Superior numbers, (297). Proceeding as in §46, maximise d_r(N)/N^ε. [Mine:] the λ-th power of p is worth including exactly when 1 + r/λ ≥ p^ε, i.e. p ≤ (1 + r/λ)^{1/ε}. Writing x = 1/ε gives
N = exp(Σ_λ ϑ((1 + r/λ)^x)).
The next page then gives d_r(N) = ∏_λ (1 + r/λ)^{π((1+r/λ)^x)}. Note that ϑ(1+r)^x means ϑ((1+r)^x).

The purpose is to obtain the maximal order of d_r(N), the analogue of the d(N) theory of §§43–46.
errors: d_{-1}(N)=0 holds only for N>1; d_{-1}(1)=1.
(296) d_r(N) ≤ 1+r fails at N=1 when -1 ≤ r < 0, since d_r(1)=1 > 1+r. It should read N>1.
The restriction 'provided r > -1' is unnecessary for (295): the binomial formula holds for all real (indeed complex) r. Presumably the restriction is there for positivity or for the later discussion.

'It can easily be shown' that maximisers have the form exp(Σϑ(x_λ)) is a sketch. Strictly, it is the superior (ε-optimal) numbers that have exactly the form (297), not every number of maximal order. This is standard in Ramanujan's framework.

deep.surprise_reason: This page belongs to the suppressed portion of Ramanujan's 1915 'Highly composite numbers' memoir. That portion was published with annotations by Nicolas and Robin (Ramanujan J. 1, 1997), so the generalisation to d_r is already known as his. The content is a natural extension of his superior highly composite method.

transcription_corrections: In (297), the image's ϑ(1+r)^x denotes ϑ((1+r)^x), with the power inside the argument of ϑ; the same holds for the other terms. The transcription's typography is ambiguous on this point.
The transcription is otherwise faithful to the image.
